reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening emergency caused by immune destruction of transfused red cells, most severely from ABO incompatibility due to clerical or identification errors
Symptoms begin during or soon after transfusion and include fever, chills, back or flank pain, pain along the infusion vein, dyspnoea, hypotension, and dark urine
In an unconscious or anaesthetised patient, unexplained hypotension, haemoglobinuria, and diffuse bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation may be the only clues
The immediate action is to stop the transfusion, keep the intravenous line open with saline, and recheck all patient and unit identifiers
The mechanism is largely intravascular haemolysis from complement-fixing IgM antibodies, releasing free haemoglobin and triggering DIC, shock, and acute kidney injury

Investigation includes repeat clerical checks, a direct antiglobulin test, inspection of plasma and urine for free haemoglobin, and haemolysis markers, with return of the unit to the transfusion service

Management is supportive with aggressive fluids to maintain renal perfusion and urine output, treatment of hypotension, and correction of coagulopathy, while prevention rests on rigorous bedside identification
reference.pathophysiology: Acute haemolytic transfusion reactions occur when recipient antibodies bind antigens on transfused red cells, most dangerously when preformed anti-A or anti-B react with ABO-incompatible cells. These IgM antibodies activate complement fully, causing rapid intravascular lysis and release of free haemoglobin. Complement fragments and cytokines produce fever, vasodilatation, and hypotension, while the reaction activates coagulation and can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation. Free haemoglobin, hypotension, and renal vasoconstriction combine to cause acute kidney injury. The severity relates to the volume of incompatible cells infused, so early recognition and cessation are critical.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial contamination of the component with septic shock
additionalInvestigations: Immediate clerical recheck of patient identity and unit labelling
Direct antiglobulin test and repeat ABO grouping on pre- and post-transfusion samples
Inspection of plasma and urine for free haemoglobin
Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, and haptoglobin
Coagulation screen and renal function to detect DIC and acute kidney injury, with cultures if sepsis is possible
redFlags: Fever, hypotension, back or flank pain, and dark urine during transfusion, indicating an acute haemolytic emergency
Unexplained intraoperative hypotension, oozing, and haemoglobinuria under anaesthesia
Evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation or oliguric acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the volume of incompatible blood transfused and the speed of response; stopping early limits harm, whereas large-volume ABO-incompatible transfusion can cause fatal shock, DIC, and renal failure.
pitfalls: Skipping or rushing the bedside identity check, the commonest root cause
Dismissing early fever or discomfort as a benign febrile reaction and continuing the transfusion
Failing to maintain intravenous access and fluids after stopping, delaying renal protection
Overlooking haemolysis in an anaesthetised patient where classic symptoms are masked
